tips: Read it in two large parts. Chapters 1–39 mostly address Judah in Isaiah's own day under the threat of Assyria; chapters 40–66 speak comfort to God's people in and after the Babylonian exile.
Learn Isaiah's favorite name for God, "the Holy One of Israel." It starts with his vision of God's holiness in the temple (Isaiah 6:1–8), which shapes the whole book.
Watch for the four Servant Songs (Isaiah 42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; Isaiah 52:13–53:12). They describe a servant of the LORD who suffers for the sins of others.

looksBack.title: The kings of Judah
looksBack.text: Isaiah ministers during the reigns told in 2 Kings 15–20; chapters 36–39 retell Hezekiah's deliverance from Assyria almost word for word from 2 Kings 18–20.

looksAhead.title: The suffering servant
looksAhead.text: Philip explains Isaiah 53:7–8 to the Ethiopian official and "preached unto him Jesus" (Acts 8:32–35), and Peter quotes the same chapter: "by whose stripes ye were healed" (1 Peter 2:24).

looksAhead.title: Jesus' first sermon
looksAhead.text: In Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2 and declares, "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears" (Luke 4:16–21).

looksAhead.title: New heavens and a new earth
looksAhead.text: Isaiah's promise of "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17) is taken up in the Bible's closing vision (Revelation 21:1).

tips: Don't expect strict chronological order. The book is a collection of messages and stories from forty years, arranged partly by theme; the kings named in each section help you place it.
Read Jeremiah's personal laments (such as Jeremiah 20:7–18). He is often called the weeping prophet because he grieves over the judgment he must announce and suffers rejection for it.
Look for the hope in the middle of the book: chapters 30–33, sometimes called the Book of Consolation, which include the promise of a new covenant.

looksBack.title: Josiah's reform
looksBack.text: Jeremiah's call comes in the thirteenth year of Josiah (Jeremiah 1:2), shortly before the discovery of the book of the law in the temple (2 Kings 22:3–13).

looksBack.title: The covenant curses
looksBack.text: Jeremiah's warnings draw heavily on the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28–30, which he sees coming true.

looksAhead.title: The new covenant
looksAhead.text: The promise of a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34) is quoted in full in Hebrews 8:8–12, and Jesus speaks of "the new testament in my blood" at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).

looksAhead.title: Seventy years
looksAhead.text: Jeremiah's prophecy that the exile would last seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10) is cited when Cyrus lets the exiles return (Ezra 1:1) and is studied by Daniel (Daniel 9:2).

tips: Read it slowly and aloud if you can. It is five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction, and its structure—acrostics in chapters 1–4—gives order to overwhelming sorrow.
Notice the center of the book, Lamentations 3:22–23: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Hope appears in the middle of grief, not after it.
Let it teach you to lament. The book does not hide pain or rush to answers; it brings honest grief and confession to God and ends with a prayer (chapter 5).

looksBack.title: The fall of Jerusalem
looksBack.text: The poems mourn the events of 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52: the siege, the famine, and the burning of the temple.

looksAhead.title: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem
looksAhead.text: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its destruction again (Luke 19:41–44).

looksAhead.title: No more tears
looksAhead.text: The Bible's final vision answers the tears of Lamentations: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes" (Revelation 21:4).

tips: Keep the date in mind. Ezekiel is already in Babylon among the exiles; Jerusalem falls partway through the book (Ezekiel 33:21), and his message shifts from judgment to hope at that point.
Read the visions as visions. Ezekiel's strange imagery—living creatures, wheels, dry bones—is meant to overwhelm and convey God's glory and power, not to be decoded detail by detail.
Follow the glory of God through the book: it appears in Babylon (chapter 1), leaves the temple in Jerusalem (chapters 10–11), and returns to a new temple (chapter 43).

looksBack.title: The first exiles
looksBack.text: Ezekiel was taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10–16; Ezekiel 1:2), about ten years before Jerusalem was destroyed.

looksAhead.title: The good shepherd
looksAhead.text: God's promise to shepherd his people himself (Ezekiel 34:11–16, 23) lies behind Jesus' words, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11).

looksAhead.title: A new heart and spirit
looksAhead.text: The promise of a new heart and God's Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26–27) is echoed when Jesus speaks of being born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5).

looksAhead.title: The river of life
looksAhead.text: The river flowing from the temple with healing trees on its banks (Ezekiel 47:1–12) reappears in Revelation 22:1–2.

tips: Read it in two halves. Chapters 1–6 are stories of Daniel and his friends staying faithful in a foreign court; chapters 7–12 are Daniel's visions of empires rising and falling.
Watch the book's main message: "the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men" (Daniel 4:17). Kings who seem all-powerful are shown to be under God's authority.
Approach the visions with humility. Their beasts and numbers have been interpreted in many ways; focus first on what is clear—God's kingdom will outlast and replace every human empire (Daniel 2:44).

looksBack.title: The first deportation
looksBack.text: Daniel is taken to Babylon in the third year of Jehoiakim (Daniel 1:1–6), during the events described in 2 Kings 24:1.

looksAhead.title: The Son of man
looksAhead.text: Daniel's vision of "one like the Son of man" receiving an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14) is behind Jesus' favorite title for himself and his words at his trial (Mark 14:62).

looksAhead.title: The resurrection
looksAhead.text: Daniel 12:2 is one of the clearest Old Testament statements of resurrection, and Jesus echoes it in John 5:28–29.

looksAhead.title: Revelation's visions
looksAhead.text: Revelation draws heavily on Daniel's imagery, including the beast from the sea (Revelation 13:1–2; Daniel 7:3–7).
